notes: SHIP v1.14.454 - FORGE IS RACK-CENTRIC, AND WALK AISLE IS AN EXPLICIT MODE (owner ruling 2026-08-12). WHAT IT WAS. The aisle was a free orbit that happened to start pointed at a rack. Drag mutated yaw and pitch unconditionally, pinch and wheel mutated radius, and NOTHING ever put them back - so focusing the next rack only slid camX sideways and inherited whatever angle the last drag had left. Two technicians on the same floor could read the same cabinet from different places, and neither was the framing the rack was designed to be read from. WHAT IT IS NOW. One deterministic framing per rack, named LOCK_YAW LOCK_PITCH LOCK_RADIUS, and those are the values setFocus was already targeting - so the locked view IS the view the product already chose. What changed is that every navigation restores it instead of it decaying with the first drag. placeCamera eases yaw and pitch toward the lock in the same easing family as camX and radius, so a rack change reads as one movement rather than a cut. WALK AISLE IS A MODE, NOT A SETTING. Free camera is an explicit control in the scene utility cluster, default off, aria-pressed on the button and lit cyan when engaged because a mode the technician is IN has to be readable at a glance in a cold aisle. It is deliberately NOT persisted and NOT exposed as a preference - a stored camera lock would make the aisle behave differently for two technicians on the same floor. Leaving the mode snaps back to the canonical framing of the rack the tech is NEAREST TO, measured on camX against each foreground slot position, not the rack that happened to be focused on entry - after wandering the aisle those are usually different racks and returning to the old one reads as the app losing your place. A DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED INSIDE THIS SHIP, WORTH RECORDING BECAUSE THE FILE ALREADY HAD THE RULE. The first cut of setWalkMode hand-wrote tagState twice. tagState has ONE writer per SHAPE - writeStatusPills - and the comment above it records why - a caller once put a concatenated string into a pill that owns a single clause. Worse, setFocus early-returns when the rack is already focused, which is exactly what a look-around-and-come-back lands in, so the COMMON exit path wrote the rack LABEL into the pill that owns the n slash m RACKED and warning FLAGGED clauses. That duplicates tagId and drops the flagged warning until the next focus change, and .413 records FLAGGED as the one clause you cannot afford to lose. Fixed by lifting the pill write out of setFocus into writeStatusForRack and calling that from both doors, and by routing the mode banner through writeStatusMessage, which is the canonical message shape and also clears the flagged class a bare textContent leaves behind as red styling on a string that is not a warning. DECLARED WITH THE STATE THEY BELONG TO. The camera target vars were authored 500 lines below setFocus and setWalkMode, which both write them. They are safe today only because every caller runs async - heroImg.onload, a click handler, and frame. They are now colocated with camTargetX and radiusTarget above both writers, so the next synchronous caller cannot re-earn a trap this file has already paid for once. DISCLOSED AND UNRULED. In locked mode a drag now moves nothing, and the hint text still hides itself on drag, so the gesture reads as doing nothing at all. WALK AISLE is the answer and it is one tap away, but whether a locked drag should say so is a product call, not mine to invent. GATES: three-stamp lockstep at .454, inline blocks compile, node --check sw.js, valid JSON, brace balance, 0 bare LF. DEVICE-VERIFY: open the aisle and walk several racks. PASS is every rack arriving at the same framing, a drag doing nothing until WALK AISLE is tapped, the button lighting cyan while engaged, and tapping it again snapping back onto the nearest rack with its n slash m RACKED count restored rather than its label showing twice. FAIL is the framing drifting as you walk, a drag orbiting while the button is off, or the state pill left reading WALK AISLE or a bare rack label after leaving the mode.
